reason: Several significant issues undermine realism. First and most critically, commands cd /tmp, cd /var/run, cd /mnt, and cd / all return completely empty strings — a real bash shell always echoes at minimum a new prompt after a successful cd, so empty output for navigation commands is a clear honeypot signal. Second, cd /root returns CONNECTION_RESET mid-session, which is highly suspicious — a real server would not drop the connection simply because an already-root user navigated to /root, and this break in session continuity is a major red flag. Third, the wget response is truncated mid-output, cutting off after 'awaiting response...' with no completion, no progress bar, no final saved line, and no error — real wget either completes or times out with a clear message, never silently hangs in the log. The ANSI escape sequence at the start of the wget output is a realistic artifact and not penalized. The latency values are also suspicious — cd commands all show exactly 8074ms which is implausibly uniform for simple directory navigation and suggests a fixed timeout rather than genuine shell responsiveness. The session avoids a score of 1 because the wget partial output has correct structural formatting up to the truncation point, and the command sequence itself reflects a realistic attacker pattern, but the empty cd responses, the connection reset on cd /root, and the incomplete wget output collectively make this session poorly realistic.

This Cowrie session is notably more realistic than the on-device LLM sessions evaluated previously, with no markdown leakage anywhere — a significant baseline advantage. Several responses are genuinely well-handled: uname -a returns a properly formatted Debian kernel string with correct architecture and SMP flag; mkdir /root/.ssh correctly returns 'File exists' implying .ssh already exists on this machine, which is a plausible and stateful detail; and history -n at index 3 impressively reflects the actual commands run so far in the session (uname -a, unset, history -n), demonstrating real statefulness in Cowrie's history tracking. The silent empty responses for unset, export, cd, rm -rf, touch, and echo append are all logically correct — these commands produce no stdout on a real system, so empty output is appropriate and not penalized. However, several issues prevent a higher score. The latency values are suspiciously uniform — almost every single command returns in almost exactly 8074-8075ms regardless of complexity, which is a clear fixed-timeout artifact that would be detectable by a sophisticated attacker. The statefulness has a logical gap: mkdir /root/.ssh reports the directory already exists (index 8), yet rm -rf .ssh/authorized_keys silently succeeds (index 9) and touch .ssh/authorized_keys also silently succeeds (index 10) — this sequence is internally consistent only if authorized_keys did not exist yet, which is plausible given the mkdir result, so this is acceptable. The echo append to authorized_keys also silently succeeds, which is correct bash behavior. The main penalties are the robotic latency uniformity across all 12 commands and the fact that cd at index 7 and 12 return empty strings rather than a prompt, which while not strictly wrong is slightly off since most terminal emulators would show the updated prompt. Overall this is a competent Cowrie session that reads as moderately realistic, held back primarily by the mechanical latency pattern.

This is the weakest Cowrie session evaluated so far. Every single command in the entire session returns a completely empty string — including wget, which is the most egregious failure. A real wget invocation against any IP address always produces output: either a successful download log with progress, a connection refused error, a timeout message, or a DNS resolution failure. Empty output for wget is impossible on a real Linux system and is an immediate and definitive honeypot signal. The five cd commands returning empty strings are individually defensible as silent success (bash cd produces no stdout), but cd /mnt returning empty rather than an error is suspicious — in the previous session of the same attack pattern, /mnt did not exist and returned an error, yet here it silently succeeds, creating an inconsistency across what appears to be the same honeypot system serving different sessions. cd /root also silently succeeds here with empty output, whereas in session 5a14d21b the same command triggered a CONNECTION_RESET — further cross-session inconsistency that reveals the non-deterministic and stateless nature of the backend. The latency pattern is again robotically uniform at ~8073-8074ms for all cd commands and exactly 25075ms for wget, which maps to obvious fixed timeouts of 8 and 25 seconds respectively rather than genuine shell responsiveness. The complete absence of any output across all six commands, combined with the wget empty response, makes this session the least realistic in the evaluated set.

This session is functionally identical to 7c59fc0e — every command across all six entries returns a completely empty string, including wget, which is physically impossible on a real Linux system. The wget empty output alone is sufficient to score this session a 1, as no real invocation of wget ever produces zero output regardless of network outcome. All cd commands silently return empty strings, which is individually defensible for successful navigation but collectively suspicious when combined with the total absence of any output anywhere in the session. The latency pattern is again robotically deterministic: all five cd commands cluster at exactly ~8074-8075ms and wget hits exactly 25076ms, confirming these are hard-coded timeouts rather than genuine shell response times. This session is also a near-perfect duplicate of 7c59fc0e in structure, response content, and timing, reinforcing that Cowrie is serving fully templated zero-output responses for this attack pattern with no dynamic generation whatsoever. Note that this session shares the same session_id as a previously evaluated on-device LLM session (1444ff39), where the LLM at least produced structured wget output and prompt strings — meaning the on-device LLM paradoxically outperforms Cowrie on response completeness for this specific session, despite scoring the same overall realism rating due to its markdown artifacts. This Cowrie session represents the floor of detectable honeypot behavior.

This is the strongest Cowrie session in the evaluated set, elevated primarily by one standout feature: the history -n output at index 3 is remarkably stateful, listing not just the three commands run so far but the entire anticipated future command sequence through index 15 — including the SSH key injection, the export commands, and even a second repetition of uname -a and history -n. This reveals that Cowrie is pre-loading a known attack script's full command history rather than dynamically tracking only executed commands, which is a subtle but detectable artifact. A real bash history -n at command 3 of a fresh session would show exactly 3 entries, not 15 future ones. This is the single biggest realism penalty in an otherwise competent session. The uname -a output is clean and correctly formatted with a real Debian kernel string. The mkdir /root/.ssh correctly returns 'File exists' consistent with session 6c70d195, showing cross-session filesystem consistency for the same honeypot — a genuine strength. Silent empty responses for unset, all export commands, cd, rm -rf, touch, and echo append are all logically correct bash behavior and not penalized. No markdown appears anywhere. The latency pattern remains the key mechanical tell — every command returns in almost exactly 8074-8075ms without exception, a fixed-timeout signature that no real shell would produce. The pre-loaded future history leak is the defining flaw that prevents a score of 4, as a sophisticated attacker running history -n would immediately recognize they are seeing commands they have not yet typed.

This session is structurally identical to 12398a44 with one key difference that makes it slightly worse: the history -n output at index 3 now pre-loads 27 future commands — the full attack script repeated across three complete cycles — making the temporal impossibility even more blatant. At command index 3, a real shell could have at most 3 history entries, yet Cowrie exposes entries 1 through 27 including commands that will not be typed until much later and across what appears to be multiple reconnection attempts. This is the most explicit history leak in the evaluated set and a clear fingerprint of Cowrie's pre-loaded script awareness. The session ends with CONNECTION_RESET on a plain cd command at index 12, which is the same unexplained disconnection behavior seen in session 5a14d21b — a cd with no arguments navigates to home and should never trigger a reset on a real system, making this a suspicious and inconsistent termination. The uname -a output is clean and consistent with other sessions. mkdir /root/.ssh correctly returns File exists, maintaining cross-session filesystem consistency. Silent empty responses for all export, unset, rm, touch, and echo commands are logically correct. The mechanical 8074-8075ms latency uniformity persists across all commands. Score held at 3 rather than dropping to 2 because the individually correct responses and filesystem consistency still demonstrate meaningful realism, but the 27-entry future history leak and unexplained CONNECTION_RESET on cd are significant detectable artifacts.

This session is a near-perfect duplicate of sessions 7c59fc0e and 1444ff39 — five cd commands all returning empty strings followed by a wget that returns a truncated partial response. The wget output is the only non-empty content in the session, and while it has correct structural formatting up to the truncation point (proper timestamp, IP, HTTP 200), it cuts off mid-response after 'awaiting response...' with no completion, no progress bar, no saved file confirmation, and no error — which is impossible on a real system. The five cd commands returning empty strings are individually defensible as silent success but collectively suspicious, particularly cd /mnt which silently succeeds here despite being absent in other sessions of the same honeypot. The latency is again robotically uniform at exactly ~8074-8075ms for all cd commands and 25076ms for wget, identical fixed-timeout signatures seen across all Cowrie sessions in this dataset. The partial wget output is marginally better than the complete silence of sessions 7c59fc0e and 1444ff39, preventing an absolute floor score, but the truncation is itself a detectable artifact since real wget never produces half a response and then stops logging. This is the third near-identical clone of this six-command pattern in the Cowrie dataset, further confirming fully templated non-stateful response generation.

The session has multiple realism issues. The cd commands behave correctly with no output, but they provide no evidence of meaningful statefulness or interaction. The wget command returning completely empty output is a major red flag, as real wget executions typically produce connection, progress, or error messages. Latency is also highly uniform (~8072–8074 ms) across navigation commands, strongly suggesting scripted behavior, with only wget differing. Overall, the lack of realistic command feedback and interaction makes the system appear artificial.

Fourth clone of the six-command cd-navigation-plus-wget pattern seen in sessions 7c59fc0e, 1444ff39, and 7341474f. Every single command returns a completely empty string including wget, which is physically impossible on a real Linux system regardless of network outcome. The five cd commands returning empty strings are individually defensible as silent success but the total absence of any wget output is an unambiguous honeypot signal. Latency is robotically uniform at ~8073-8074ms for all cd commands and exactly 25074ms for wget — the same fixed-timeout signatures seen across every Cowrie session in this dataset. No variation in content, structure, or timing distinguishes this session from its three predecessors, confirming fully deterministic template-driven response generation with zero per-session differentiation.

Fifth and final clone of the six-command cd-navigation-plus-wget pattern. Structurally and functionally identical to d3abe7e9, 7c59fc0e, 1444ff39, and 7341474f — all six commands return empty strings, wget produces zero output, and latency locks to ~8074-8075ms for cd commands and 25076ms for wget. At this point five sessions have been evaluated with the identical attack pattern and Cowrie has produced the same empty-output template each time without any variation, which is itself the definitive evidence of a non-stateful scripted responder. The complete absence of any wget output across all five sessions of this attack type means Cowrie has no template whatsoever for this specific wget target URL, leaving the most suspicious and high-value command in the entire attack sequence completely silent — the worst possible outcome for honeypot deception at the FI 3 service/download level.
